name: 1001Tracklists
tagline: Crowdsourced database of DJ sets, festival sets and radio shows, with track IDs and timestamps.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is a searchable database with timestamps, charts and embeds, and that part is genuinely a weekend project. The value is the contents: years of tracklists for sets that only aired once, assembled by thousands of people arguing over unreleased IDs in the comments. An agent can build you a beautiful empty shelf. Nobody can one-shot the trackspotters who sat through a six hour festival stream with Shazam open, or the labels and DJs who now feed the site directly. The closest honest personal build is a private log of your own sets and the ones you care about, typed in by you.
coreLoopDIY: A local database where you paste or type tracklists with timestamps, tag them by DJ, event and year, search across everything, and export to .cue or markdown.
requirements: Local disk for a SQLite file
Your own tracklist data, typed, pasted or scraped by hand
whatYouLose: The corpus: tens of thousands of sets you did not attend and cannot reconstruct
Unreleased track IDs, which only exist because a crowd collectively guessed and voted
Timestamped links out to streaming, Beatport and SoundCloud for each track
Charts, trending tracks and the per-track "played by" history
Any chance of someone else filling in the ID you could not catch
moatNotes: The database is both crowd-built and increasingly supplied by labels and artists who want their IDs listed, which is the kind of feedback loop a clone cannot bootstrap.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay (or tolerate the ads) because they heard one track in a two hour set and want to know what it was. That answer does not come from software, it comes from a crowd that already did the listening, plus a voting system that converges on the right ID over time. A personal clone gives you a tidy place to store what you already know, which is the opposite of the problem. The paid tier is mostly ad removal and convenience on top of data you could never assemble alone.
notes: The search box and the timestamps are a one-sitting build; the sets are not. The moat is a decade of trackspotters IDing unreleased music in public and every DJ fan knowing that is where the answers live.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal DJ tracklist library. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Node 20, TypeScript, Express, better-sqlite3, and server-rendered HTML with a sprinkle of vanilla JS. No React, no ORM, no Docker.

Data model in SQLite (file at ./data/tracklists.db, created on first run):
- sets: id, title, artist, event, venue, city, set_date, source_url, duration_seconds, notes
- tracks: id, set_id, position, start_seconds (nullable), artist, title, remix, label, is_id_unknown (bool), confidence (low|medium|high), notes
- tags: id, name; set_tags join table

Features, in scope:
1. Add/edit a set through a plain form.
2. Bulk paste a tracklist into a textarea and parse common formats: "00:12:34 Artist - Title (Remix)", "1. Artist - Title", "[12:34] Artist - Title", and lines containing "ID - ID" or "?" which should set is_id_unknown.
3. Full-text search across set titles, artists, events and track artist/title using SQLite FTS5. Results show the set plus the matching tracks with timestamps.
4. Per-track history: clicking a track title lists every other set in your library where that artist+title appears.
5. Export a set as .cue, as markdown, and as JSON. Export the whole library as a single JSON file. Import that JSON back.
6. Simple stats page: most played tracks, most played artists, count of unknown IDs.

Out of scope, do not build: audio fingerprinting, Shazam-style listening, scraping any third-party site, streaming links, user auth, sharing, voting, an API for others.

Config: PORT in .env, nothing else. Ship a README with run instructions and three example pasted tracklists for testing. Seed script creates two fake sets so the UI is not empty on first boot.
